📊 1. Etiology &
Types of Gallstones
Epidemiology

Classic patient profile follows the 4 Fs:
Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile
Cholesterol Stones (75-80%)

Formed when bile is supersaturated with cholesterol
relative to bile salts and lecithin

Reduced Bile Salts:
From liver diseases or malabsorption
(e.g., Crohn's disease, terminal ileal resection)

Increased Cholesterol Secretion:
Obesity, high dietary fat, hyperlipidemia,
and estrogen (pregnancy, OCP use)

Biliary Stasis / Impaired Emptying:
Induced by progesterone, diabetic neuropathy,
truncal vagotomy, or prolonged TPN
Pigment Stones (20-25%)
Driven by excess unconjugated bilirubin

Black Stones (from Blood):
Hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disorders, liver cirrhosis

Brown Stones (from Bacteria):
Chronic infection/stasis, biliary pathogens produce
beta-glucuronidase (hydrolyzes bilirubin)
🩺 2. Clinical Spectrum
Silent (Asymptomatic)
Accidentally discovered in 70% of cases

Management: Observation
Prophylactic cholecystectomy only for high risk
(porcelain gallbladder, diabetics, immunosuppressed)
Biliary Colic (Symptomatic)
Pathology: Transient cystic duct obstruction

Symptoms: Constant RUQ/epigastrium pain radiating to back,
precipitated by fatty meals, resolves in hours
Labs: Normal liver function tests, amylase, and lipase

Associated: Saint's Triad
(Hiatus Hernia, Peptic Ulcer, Cholelithiasis)
Management: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Acute Calcular Cholecystitis

Pathology: Persistent obstruction leading to
inflammation, edema, ischemia, and bacterial overgrowth

Symptoms: Severe constant RUQ pain > 4-6 hours,
fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis

Signs: Positive Murphy's Sign, Boas' Sign
(hyperesthesia between 9th-11th right ribs)
Progression: Mucocele, Empyema (Pyocele), Gangrene, Perforation

Management:
Early ( 3d): Conservative (Rule of 6Rs), interval surgery in 6 weeks
Acute Acalculous Cholecystitis

Pathology: Absence of stones. Seen in ICU,
driven by bile stasis and gallbladder ischemia

Management: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
Percutaneous cholecystostomy tube if unstable
Emphysematous Cholecystitis

Pathology: Gas-forming bacteria (Clostridium).
Common in elderly diabetic males

Management: Emergent cholecystectomy
due to high risk of gangrene and rapid perforation
🚨 3. Complications of Migration
Choledocholithiasis (Stones in CBD)
Pathology: Stone migrates to CBD causing biliary obstruction

Symptoms: RUQ pain, fluctuating obstructive jaundice
(pale/clay stools, dark urine)

Diagnostics: Elevated AP and GGT out of proportion.
Ultrasound shows dilated intra/extrahepatic biliary radicals

Management:
1. ERCP (sphincterotomy and stone extraction)
2. Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (3-7 days later)
3. Open Choledocholithotomy with T-Tube (if ERCP fails)
Acute Ascending Cholangitis

Pathology: CBD obstruction leads to rapid
ascending bacterial infection into liver

Presentation:
Charcot's Triad (Fever with rigors, RUQ pain, Jaundice)
Reynold's Pentad (+ Hypotension, Altered mental status)

Management:
IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Emergent biliary decompression (ERCP or PTC)
Cholecystectomy delayed until sepsis resolves
Acute Gallstone Pancreatitis

Pathology: Stone impaction at ampulla of Vater
blocking pancreatic duct, causing autodigestion

Symptoms: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating through to back.
Elevated serum amylase (> 1000 IU/dL) and lipase

Management: Supportive care (fluids, analgesics, bowel rest).
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during same admission
Mirizzi's Syndrome

Pathology: Large stone impacted in gallbladder neck/Hartmann's pouch
externally compresses Common Hepatic Duct (CHD)

Surgical Danger: Stone can erode forming fistulous cavity.
CHD can be accidentally ligated during surgery
Gallstone Ileus

Pathology: Large stone (> 2.5cm) erodes into duodenum (fistula),
impacts at terminal ileum causing mechanical small bowel obstruction
Symptoms: Intermittent tumbling obstruction (pain, nausea, vomiting)

Rigler's Triad: Small bowel obstruction,
Pneumobilia, Radiopaque gallstone in right iliac fossa

Management: Urgent laparotomy and enterotomy to extract stone.
Leave gallbladder and fistula alone during emergency
🔍 4. Diagnostic Workup
Abdominal Ultrasound (U/S)
First-line screening tool of choice (95% accuracy)

Symptomatic Cholelithiasis: Acoustic shadowing,
normal gallbladder wall and normal CBD

Acute Cholecystitis: Wall thickening > 4mm,
pericholecystic fluid, positive sonographic Murphy's sign
HIDA Scan (Cholescintigraphy)

Most sensitive diagnostic test for acute cholecystitis
if ultrasound is equivocal

Positive finding: Gallbladder fails to visualize
(cystic duct is obstructed)
MRCP
Non-invasive standard for detailed anatomical mapping of biliary tree
Highly diagnostic for choledocholithiasis, biliary strictures, cysts
ERCP

Primarily a therapeutic modality for extracting CBD stones,
dilating strictures, or placing stents

Complications: Bleeding/hemobilia (2-9%),
post-ERCP pancreatitis (1-4%), acute ascending cholangitis (1-3%)
⚠️ 5. Post-Operative Complications
Common Bile Duct (CBD) Injury
Most feared complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Occurs when CBD is mistaken for cystic duct and divided

Consequences: Bile leaks (bilomas), chronic strictures,
recurrent cholangitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis
Treatment: Urgent reconstruction via Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
Postcholecystectomy Syndrome (PCS)
Recurrent or persistent RUQ pain and biliary symptoms after surgery

Causes: Retained/missed CBD stone, long cystic duct stump,
sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, gastritis/peptic ulcer disease
